summary: Describes a schema for storing user passwords in an LDAP directory, including the authPassword attribute type. It supports password-based user authentication with stored values that can use different schemes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP directories normally keep passwords in an attribute that can only hold the password itself, in readable form. This memo defines a second attribute, authPassword, whose values carry a named scheme, some extra information such as a salt, and a stored value such as a hash. It also defines two ways for a client to ask whether a typed password matches what is stored.

questions: how to store passwords in ldap
what is the ldap authpassword attribute
how do ldap directories store hashed passwords
subtitle: A schema for storing passwords in an LDAP directory so that the stored form can be a hash rather than the password itself.

tldr.problem: The standard LDAP attribute for passwords can only hold the password in clear text, so a directory that wants to store a hashed password has nowhere to put it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the authPassword attribute, whose values carry a scheme name, some scheme-specific information and a scheme-specific value. It also defines two matching rules so a client can ask whether a clear text password matches, and two schemes, MD5 and SHA1, that hash the password together with a salt.
tldr.outcome: Servers that support simple bind must support the SHA1 scheme, and hashed values are still to be protected as if they were clear text passwords. The memo is Informational.

facts.label: Worked example
facts.value: User joe, password mary, salt salt, value marysalt

today: RFC 3112 is an Informational memo and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It describes the authPassword attribute and its two matching rules, and says that servers which support simple bind must support the SHA1 scheme. It is read with RFC 2252 for the LDAP attribute syntax definitions and RFC 2829 for LDAP authentication methods.

sections.title: Background and Intended Use
sections.content:
The userPassword attribute type is intended to support the LDAP simple bind operation, in which a client proves its identity by giving a name and a password. However, values of userPassword must be clear text passwords, and it is often desirable to store values derived from the user's password instead of the actual password.

The authPassword attribute type is intended to store the information used to implement simple password based authentication, and may be used by LDAP servers to implement the simple authentication method of the bind operation. The attribute type supports multiple storage schemes. A matching rule is provided for use with extensible search filters, allowing clients to assert that a clear text password matches one of the attribute's values.

Storage schemes often use cryptographic strength one-way hashing. The memo notes that hashing reduces the potential that exposed values will allow unauthorized access to the directory, unless the hash algorithm or its implementation is flawed, and that the hashing of passwords is intended to be an additional layer of protection. It is RECOMMENDED that hashed values be protected as if they were clear text passwords.

The attribute may be used in conjunction with server side password generation mechanisms, such as the LDAP Password Modify extended operation. Access to it may be governed by administrative controls, such as those that implement password change policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual LDAP password attribute stores the password itself, so anyone who can read the directory can read the passwords. This memo adds an attribute that can store a scrambled form instead, along with the rules a server needs to check a typed password against it.

sections.title: The authPassword Syntax
sections.content:
Values of the syntax are encoded according to the following structure: a scheme, then scheme-specific information, then a scheme-specific value, separated by spaces and a dollar sign. The scheme may contain the digits 0 to 9, the letters A to Z, and the characters hyphen, full stop, forward slash and underscore. The two scheme-specific fields hold printable ASCII less the dollar sign and the space.

The scheme describes the mechanism. The authInfo field is often a base64 encoded salt, and the authValue field is often a base64 encoded value derived from a user's password. Values of this attribute are case sensitive.

The syntax has the object identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.1.2. Transfer of values of this syntax is strongly discouraged where the underlying transport service cannot guarantee confidentiality, because that may result in disclosure of the values to unauthorized parties. The schema definitions are described in terms of the LDAPv3 Attribute Syntax Definitions, with the syntax itself detailed using Augmented BNF.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stored value has three parts: the name of the scheme used, the extra information that scheme needs, and the value itself. They are separated by a dollar sign and spaces, and the two scheme-specific parts can hold any printable character except those two.

sections.title: Matching Rules and Attributes
sections.content:
Two matching rules are defined. The authPasswordExactMatch rule allows a client to assert that an asserted authPasswordSyntax value matches authPasswordSyntax values, and is meant to be used as the EQUALITY matching rule of attributes whose SYNTAX is authPasswordSyntax. The assertion is TRUE if there is an attribute value which has the same scheme, authInfo and authValue components as the asserted value; FALSE if no attribute value has the same components as the asserted value; and Undefined otherwise.

The authPasswordMatch rule allows a client to assert that a password matches values of authPasswordSyntax using an extensibleMatch filter component. Each value is matched according to its own scheme. The assertion is TRUE if one or more attribute values match the asserted value, FALSE if all values do not match, and Undefined otherwise. Servers which support use of this matching rule SHOULD publish appropriate matchingRuleUse values. Transfer of authPasswordMatch assertion values is strongly discouraged where the underlying transport service cannot guarantee confidentiality.

Two attributes complete the schema. supportedAuthPasswordSchemes holds the names of the authentication password schemes the server supports, may only be present in the root DSE, and is not present at all if the server supports no password schemes. authPassword holds the values that are representative of the user's passwords and may be used for authentication purposes; transfer of these values is also strongly discouraged where the transport cannot guarantee confidentiality. A helper object class, authPasswordObject, allows entries of that class to contain authPassword attribute types.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways to check a password are provided. The exact rule compares the three stored parts, so it only matches a value built the same way. The general rule lets the server check each stored value according to the scheme it was written in. The server also publishes a list of the schemes it supports.

sections.title: The MD5 and SHA1 Schemes
sections.content:
The memo describes two schemes. Schemes which are not described in an RFC SHOULD be named with a leading X-, to indicate a private or implementation specific scheme, or may be named using the dotted-decimal representation of an object identifier assigned to the scheme.

The MD5 scheme is named MD5. Its authValue is the base64 encoding of an MD5 digest of the concatenation of the user password and the salt, and the base64 encoding of the salt is provided in the authInfo field. The salt MUST be at least 64 bits long, and implementations of this scheme MUST support salts up to 128 bits in length. The worked example: given a user joe whose password is mary and a salt of salt, the authInfo field would be the base64 encoding of salt, and the authValue field would be the base64 encoding of the MD5 digest of marysalt. A match against an asserted password and an attribute value of this scheme SHALL be true if and only if the MD5 digest of the concatenation of the asserted value and the salt is equal to the MD5 digest contained in the authValue. The match SHALL be undefined if the server is unable to complete the equality test for any reason, and otherwise it SHALL be false. Values of this scheme SHOULD only be used to implement simple user and password authentication.

The SHA1 scheme is named SHA1 and works in the same way, with a SHA1 digest in place of the MD5 digest and the same salt length requirements. Its worked example uses the same user joe, password mary and salt salt, so the authInfo field is again the base64 encoding of salt and the authValue field is the base64 encoding of the SHA1 digest of marysalt.
sections.plainLanguage: Two schemes are defined. In each, the server hashes the password with a salt and stores the result, so the password itself is never written down. The salt must be at least 64 bits long and implementations must cope with salts of 128 bits.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Servers MAY restrict which schemes are used in conjunction with a particular authentication process, but SHOULD use all values of the selected schemes. If the asserted password matches any of the stored values, the asserted password SHOULD be considered valid. Servers MAY use other authentication storage mechanisms, such as userPassword or an external password store, in conjunction with authPassword to support the authentication process.

Servers that support simple bind MUST support the SHA1 scheme and SHOULD support the MD5 scheme. Servers SHOULD NOT publish values of authPassword, nor allow operations which expose authPassword values or authPasswordMatch assertions, unless confidentiality protection is in place. Clients SHOULD NOT initiate operations which provide or request values of authPassword, or make authPasswordMatch assertions, unless confidentiality protection is in place.

One point is worth stating on its own: clients SHOULD NOT assume that a successful authPasswordMatch, whether by compare or by search, is sufficient to gain directory access. The bind operation MUST be used to authenticate to the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may support only some schemes, but it should check every value it holds for a chosen scheme. Servers and clients should keep the attribute off the wire unless the connection is protected. And a successful password check is not a login: the client still has to bind to the directory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authentication information MUST be adequately protected, because unintended disclosure will allow attackers to gain immediate access to the directory. As flaws may be discovered in the hashing algorithm or with a particular implementation of it, and because values could be subject to various attacks if exposed, values of authPassword SHOULD be protected as if they were clear text passwords. When values are transferred, privacy protections such as IPSEC or TLS SHOULD be in place. Clients SHOULD use strong authentication mechanisms.

The authPasswordMatch matching rule allows applications to test the validity of a user password and, hence, may be used to mount an attack. Servers SHOULD take appropriate measures to protect the directory from such attacks. Some password schemes may require CPU intensive operations, so servers SHOULD take appropriate measures to protect against Denial of Service attacks.

Two further points. authPassword does not restrict an authentication identity to a single password: an attacker who gains write access to this attribute may store additional values without disabling the user's true passwords, so use of policy aware clients and servers is RECOMMENDED. And because the level of protection differs from scheme to scheme, it is RECOMMENDED that servers support scheme selection as a configuration item, which allows a scheme to be disabled if a significant security flaw is discovered.
sections.plainLanguage: A stored hash still has to be kept out of reach, because exposing it gives attackers a direct way in. The matching rule is itself a way to attack a directory by guessing passwords one at a time, and some schemes cost the server a lot of processor time. The memo recommends making the scheme a configurable choice, so a broken scheme can be switched off.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAX DEFINITION AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: authPasswordValue
data.code:
authPasswordValue = w scheme s authInfo s authValue w
scheme = %x30-39 / %x41-5A / %x2D-2F / %x5F
      ; 0-9, A-Z, "-", ".", "/", or "_"
authInfo = schemeSpecificValue
authValue = schemeSpecificValue
        schemeSpecificValue = *( %x21-23 / %x25-7E )
      ; printable ASCII less "$" and " "
s = w SEP w
w = *SP
SEP = %x24 ; "$"
SP = %x20 ; " " (space)

viz.caption: THE TWO SCHEMES THE MEMO DEFINES

cells: Base64 encoding of an MD5 digest of the password concatenated with the salt
Base64 encoding of a SHA1 digest of the password concatenated with the salt
Base64 encoding of the salt, in authInfo

viz.caption: THE RULES THE MEMO SETS FOR SERVERS AND CLIENTS

items.title: Simple bind
items.text: Servers MUST support the SHA1 scheme and SHOULD support the MD5 scheme.

items.title: Publishing values
items.text: Servers SHOULD NOT publish authPassword values without confidentiality protection.

items.title: Client requests
items.text: Clients SHOULD NOT request or assert authPassword values without confidentiality protection.

items.title: Getting access
items.text: A successful match is not access; the bind operation MUST be used to authenticate.
